arabic_grammar_name: clitic + host (sawābiq wa-lawāḥiq)
plain_rule: A written Arabic word may carry a prefixed particle (wāw, fāʾ, bāʾ, kāf, lām, or the article al-); its contribution is part of the meaning and must be shown, not hidden inside the host word.
trigger_condition: the token begins with a legal proclitic sequence
expected_feature: proclitic + host shown separately
typical_error_feature: the whole token read as one stem
point_template: Look again at the start of this word: it may begin with a small attached particle.
teach_template: When a word starts with wāw/fāʾ/bāʾ/kāf/lām or al-, that piece is a separate particle with its own meaning; read the host without it, then add the particle's contribution.
bottom_out_template: Split the word into the prefixed particle and the host, and gloss each piece.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner sees a word beginning with a sun letter and still pronounces a full lam, treating every al- prefix the same regardless of the letter that follows it.
A learner reads a prefixed particle and its host as one unfamiliar word instead of separating the small attached piece from the host first.

arabic_grammar_name: attached pronoun (ḍamīr muttaṣil)
plain_rule: A pronoun attached to the end of a word (a possessive on a noun, an object on a verb) is a separate piece of meaning; a single-letter ending can also be a root letter, so without context it stays a candidate.
trigger_condition: the token ends in a possible enclitic pronoun
expected_feature: the attached pronoun surfaced, or the token kept pending
typical_error_feature: the ending folded into the stem
point_template: Look at the ending of this word: it may be an attached pronoun rather than part of the root.
teach_template: An attached pronoun at the end carries 'his/her/their/you/us'; but a lone single letter could also be a radical, so confirm from context before deciding.
bottom_out_template: Separate the enclitic pronoun from the stem and name its reference.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner treats the final letter of a word as part of the root instead of checking whether it is an attached pronoun pointing back to someone or something already mentioned.
A learner assumes an attached pronoun always matches the word it is written on, rather than the person or thing it actually refers to.

arabic_grammar_name: unvoweled ambiguity (ishtibāh ʿinda ʿadam al-tashkīl)
plain_rule: Without short vowels, the same letters can be more than one word; keep every reading as a candidate and do not pick one until evidence appears.
trigger_condition: an unvoweled token with more than one reading
expected_feature: the competing readings kept and ranked
typical_error_feature: one reading forced
point_template: These letters can be read more than one way; notice that the short vowels are missing.
teach_template: Unvoweled Arabic underdetermines the word: the same letters may be a noun or a verb. Keep the readings side by side and let context or a source decide.
bottom_out_template: List the competing readings with their ranking; do not assert one.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner picks the more familiar reading of an unvoweled word and drops the other possible reading, instead of keeping both until something in the sentence decides.

arabic_grammar_name: multi-function particle (ḥarf mutaʿaddid al-maʿnā)
plain_rule: Some particles (mā, wāw, lā, in, ...) have several functions; the function is decided by context, not by the surface form alone.
trigger_condition: the token is or contains a multi-function particle
expected_feature: the particle's function decided from context
typical_error_feature: one fixed gloss assumed
point_template: This little word has several possible jobs here; look at what surrounds it.
teach_template: A particle like mā or wāw can be negation, a relative, a question, coordination, and more; identify the function from the clause, then gloss it accordingly.
bottom_out_template: Name the particle's function in this clause and its effect.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner assigns one fixed English meaning to a small particle without checking whether the surrounding words point to a different job for it here.
A learner treats a multi-function particle as only ever a connector, missing that the same shape can mark a wish, a question, or an exception depending on the sentence.

arabic_grammar_name: preposition + genitive (jārr wa-majrūr)
plain_rule: A prefixed preposition (bāʾ, lām, kāf) forms a jar-majrūr with the following word; the relation must be shown, not the host alone.
trigger_condition: a prefixed preposition is present
expected_feature: the jar-majrūr relation shown
typical_error_feature: only the host glossed
point_template: There is a prefixed preposition here; it links to the word it governs.
teach_template: A prefixed preposition makes the following noun genitive (majrūr); read them as a phrase and show the relation.
bottom_out_template: Name the preposition and the genitive noun it governs.

arabic_grammar_name: case / mood from context (al-iʿrāb bi-ḥasab al-siyāq)
plain_rule: The case or mood ending depends on the governing element; when the ending is not visible, the reading stays a candidate until context confirms it.
trigger_condition: case/mood is not decidable from the surface
expected_feature: case/mood justified by a governor
typical_error_feature: a case asserted with no visible ending
point_template: Look at the ending here and at the word that governs it before deciding the case or mood.
teach_template: A case or mood ending is assigned by a governing element; name that governor and the case it requires, and if it is not visible, keep the reading pending.
bottom_out_template: State the governor and the case/mood it assigns.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner assigns a case ending from a general rule without checking whether the clause's polarity or structure changes which rule actually applies here.
A learner marks a noun by habit without checking whether the sentence's negation blocks that marking in this position.

arabic_grammar_name: the governing element (al-ʿāmil) justifies the iʿrāb
plain_rule: A correct ending is not enough: the governing element must justify it. A right ending with an absent or wrong governor is unsafe reasoning and goes to review.
trigger_condition: a case is asserted without a justified governor
expected_feature: the case justified by a named governor
typical_error_feature: right answer, wrong or absent reason
point_template: Name the element that governs this word before you justify its ending.
teach_template: The ending must be justified by the ʿāmil (the governing element); naming the right case with the wrong or no governor is unsafe and is routed to review, not accepted.
bottom_out_template: Identify the governor, then justify the assigned case/mood from it.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner names a correct case ending but cannot say which word or particle actually requires it, treating the right answer as its own justification.
A learner assumes the nearest word is always the one assigning the case, without checking whether an earlier element in the clause is the real governor.

arabic_grammar_name: kāna and her sisters (kāna wa-akhawātuhā)
plain_rule: Kāna and her sister verbs (kāna, laysa, ṣāra, aṣbaḥa, amsā, aḍḥā, ẓalla, bāta) keep the subject nominative but push the predicate into the accusative; a right case ending with no named kāna-family governor, or a predicate left nominative after one of these verbs, is unsafe until the governor is named.
trigger_condition: a kāna-family verb governs a nominal predication and the governor lattice cannot confirm both the subject's nominative and the predicate's accusative from the supplied evidence
expected_feature: the kāna-family verb named as governor, subject nominative, predicate accusative
typical_error_feature: the predicate left nominative, or the case pattern of a particle-headed family (inna's) applied to a verb-headed construction
point_template: Before assigning a case here, name which verb from the kāna family is doing the governing.
teach_template: Kāna and her sisters keep the subject in the nominative but push the predicate into the accusative; the predicate's case is a consequence of the verb, not a default. A right case ending named without this governor, or the predicate left nominative, is unsafe and goes to review.
bottom_out_template: Name the kāna-family verb, then justify nominative-subject/accusative-predicate from it.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner sees a kāna-family verb and leaves the following predicate nominative instead of checking that this verb pushes it into the accusative.
A learner applies inna-family's ism-accusative/khabar-nominative pattern to a kāna-headed sentence, producing both exponents wrong.

arabic_grammar_name: polarity-licensed kāna-sisters (mā zāla, mā dāma, mā fatiʾa, mā infakka)
plain_rule: Some kāna-sisters only carry their continuative sense together with a licensing negator (mā zāla = 'has not ceased' = 'is still'); dropping the licenser reverses the meaning, and mā dāma's construction additionally requires a consequent clause rather than functioning as plain sentence negation.
trigger_condition: a continuative kāna-sister appears with no supplied negative-polarity licenser, or a mā-composite is read as ordinary negation with no consequent clause
expected_feature: the licensing negator (or its confirmed absence) checked before the continuative sense is asserted
typical_error_feature: the continuative sense assumed from the bare verb, or the mā-composite treated as an ordinary sentence negator
point_template: Check whether this kāna-sister has its required licensing negator before you read it as continuative.
teach_template: Mā zāla-type members only mean 'still/continues' together with their licensing negator; the bare verb without it means the opposite (ceased). Mā dāma is a different composite again — it requires a consequent clause, not plain negation. No family expectation is applied without the licenser.
bottom_out_template: Name the licensing negator this member requires, or state that it is missing and the continuative sense is not licensed.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner reads a bare continuative verb like zāla as asserting 'still/continues' without checking for the negator that licenses that sense, so the sentence states the opposite of what was intended.

arabic_grammar_name: inna and her sisters (inna wa-akhawātuhā)
plain_rule: Inna and her sister particles (inna, anna, kaʾanna, lākinna [heavy/geminate], layta, laʿalla) push the following noun into the accusative (the ism) and keep its predicate in the nominative (the khabar) — the reverse pattern of kāna's family; a light lākin never governs, and only the geminate lākinna is a member.
trigger_condition: an inna-family particle governs a nominal predication and the ism/khabar case pattern is not confirmed from the supplied evidence, or a light/heavy or inna/anna selection is at stake
expected_feature: the ism accusative, the khabar nominative, and the correct family member (geminate vs light, inna vs anna) named
typical_error_feature: the ism left nominative, the khabar marked accusative (importing kāna's pattern), or a non-governing light lākin treated as a governor
point_template: Before assigning a case here, confirm which inna-family particle is governing and whether it is the governing (geminate) member.
teach_template: Inna and her sisters put their ism in the accusative and keep their khabar in the nominative — the mirror of kāna's pattern. Only the geminate lākinna governs; a light lākin does not. The regime must be confirmed before either case is asserted.
bottom_out_template: Name the inna-family particle, confirm it is the governing member, then justify ism-accusative/khabar-nominative from it.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner leaves an inna-family particle's ism in the nominative, missing that the whole family signature is the accusative it imposes there.
A learner treats a light, non-doubled lākin as a governing member of inna's family instead of checking the shadda first.

arabic_grammar_name: verbs of the heart (afʿāl al-qulūb) — complement count by sense
plain_rule: Cognition verbs such as ẓanna and ḥasiba take two accusative objects only in their judgemental (heart/opinion) sense; in a literal-perception or location sense the same verb takes a single object, and the two-accusative expectation is never asserted without a supplied judgemental sense.
trigger_condition: a zanna-family verb's sense (judgemental vs literal-perception) is not supplied, or a two-accusative pattern is asserted against a verb used in its literal sense, or the verb's own subject is counted as one of its objects
expected_feature: the verb's sense checked first; two accusative complements only in the judgemental sense; the subject kept separate from the complements
typical_error_feature: a two-accusative expectation forced onto a literal-perception/location use, only one complement marked accusative in a genuine judgemental use, or the subject miscounted as a complement
point_template: Before counting complements here, settle which sense this cognition verb carries.
teach_template: Ẓanna-family verbs take two accusative objects only in the judgemental sense (an opinion about how two things relate); the same verb in a literal-perception or location sense takes one object. The verb's own subject is never one of the complements. No two-accusative expectation is asserted without a supplied judgemental sense.
bottom_out_template: State the verb's sense, then the complement count and case pattern it licenses.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner forces a two-accusative-object reading onto a cognition verb used in its literal-perception sense, where it actually takes one object.
A learner counts a cognition verb's own subject as one of its two accusative complements.

arabic_grammar_name: stacked abrogators (tarākub al-nawāsikh) — scope and bracketing
plain_rule: When more than one abrogator (a kāna/inna/ẓanna-family trigger) appears in one span, each governs only its own pair of elements; without a supplied bracketing that states which governor takes scope over what, no single family's case expectation is assigned across the whole span.
trigger_condition: more than one abrogator trigger is present in the same span and the clause bracketing (which governor scopes over which elements) is not supplied
expected_feature: each governor's scope resolved separately, with no case assigned where the bracketing is unresolved
typical_error_feature: one family's signature applied across the whole span, corrupting the elements that belong to the other governor
point_template: Before assigning any case here, check how many governors are in this span and which elements belong to each.
teach_template: Each abrogator governs only its own pair; when two governors are stacked in one span, resolve each one's scope separately. Without a supplied bracketing, no case is assigned across the whole span.
bottom_out_template: Name each governor present and the elements it — and only it — governs.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner applies one governor's case signature across an entire span that actually contains two separate governors, corrupting the elements that belong to the other one.

arabic_grammar_name: orthographic variant (rasm / hamza form)
plain_rule: An orthographic variant (hamza seat, alif form, tāʾ marbūṭa, alif maqṣūra) is normalized for matching only; the original spelling is preserved and may itself be significant.
trigger_condition: an orthographic variant is present
expected_feature: original spelling preserved; match-key normalized
typical_error_feature: the variant treated as an error
point_template: Notice the spelling of this letter; it is a variant that is normalized only for matching.
teach_template: Hamza seats and alif/tāʾ forms vary in writing; the original spelling is kept, and only a match key is normalized.
bottom_out_template: Show the original spelling and the normalized match key side by side.

arabic_grammar_name: hidden proclitic in a composed token (sābiq multaṣiq lam yuḥtasab)
plain_rule: When a written token carries a prefixed particle (wāw, fāʾ, bāʾ, lām, kāf, or al-), the gloss must account for that prefix; a hover that shows only the host word has dropped a real piece of the meaning.
trigger_condition: a source-addressed hover shows only the host of a token that begins with a proclitic
expected_feature: the proclitic and the host each accounted for in the hover
typical_error_feature: the whole token glossed as the bare host
point_template: Look at the start of this word: a small attached particle is part of it, and the hover has left it out.
teach_template: A prefixed wāw/fāʾ/bāʾ/lām/kāf or al- is a separate piece with its own meaning; the hover must show the host and add the prefix's contribution, not the host alone.
bottom_out_template: Split the token into the prefixed particle and the host, and give each piece its own contribution.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A hover shows only the host word and drops a prefixed particle that changes whether the token is a question word or a preposition.

arabic_grammar_name: dropped attached pronoun (ḍamīr muttaṣil saqaṭa mina l-hover)
plain_rule: An attached pronoun at the end of a token (an object on a verb, a possessive on a noun) is part of the meaning; a gloss that drops it under-reports the token.
trigger_condition: a source-addressed hover omits a token's attached pronoun
expected_feature: the attached pronoun surfaced with its reference
typical_error_feature: the ending folded into the stem and lost
point_template: Look at the ending of this word: an attached pronoun is there, and the hover has not accounted for it.
teach_template: An attached pronoun carries 'his/her/their/you/us'; the hover must keep it and name what it refers to, not fold it into the stem.
bottom_out_template: Separate the attached pronoun from the stem and name its reference.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner reads a verb's final letter as decoration and misses that it is an object pronoun, so the object of the action disappears from the reading.
A learner keeps a possessive pronoun on a word after the following noun that licensed it has been dropped.

arabic_grammar_name: hidden passive voice (bināʾ lil-majhūl maṭwī)
plain_rule: A finite passive verb must keep its passive contribution in the gloss; reading it as active changes who does and who receives the action.
trigger_condition: a hover glosses a passive verb as active or as a bare dictionary form
expected_feature: the passive voice preserved in the gloss (e.g. 'was created', not 'created' or 'to create')
typical_error_feature: an active or infinitive gloss on a passive verb
point_template: Check the voice of this verb before glossing: it is passive, and an active reading changes the meaning.
teach_template: A passive verb reports that the action was done to its subject; keep that in the gloss ('was created', 'is said'), not an active or dictionary form.
bottom_out_template: State the verb's voice, then give a passive gloss that matches it.

arabic_grammar_name: hidden dual/plural ending (ʿalāmat tathniya aw jamʿ maṭwiyya)
plain_rule: A visible dual or plural ending carries the number; a hover that shows only a singular host, or carries the number only in English, has hidden the ending that teaches it.
trigger_condition: a hover hides a token's visible dual or plural ending
expected_feature: the dual/plural ending shown as part of the breakdown
typical_error_feature: a plain singular host span with the number carried only in English
point_template: Look at the ending of this word: it marks a dual or plural, and the hover has not shown it.
teach_template: The dual ending and the plural endings carry the number; the breakdown must show the ending, not only an English 'two' or a plain host.
bottom_out_template: Point to the dual or plural ending and name the number it marks.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner reports a noun's number only from the English translation and does not point to the ending that actually marks it as two or many.
A learner keeps a plural ending on a form after its role in the sentence changes, without checking whether that ending is still licensed there.

arabic_grammar_name: hidden derivative/participle shape (shakl al-mushtaqq maṭwī)
plain_rule: A derived noun (an active or passive participle and its kin) is not the verb; its derivative shape must be visible, and it is never glossed as a verb.
trigger_condition: a hover hides a token's derivative prefix/pattern or glosses a derivative as a verb
expected_feature: the derivative shape shown and glossed as a noun/adjective, not a verb
typical_error_feature: a verb gloss on a participle, or the derivative prefix hidden in one span
point_template: This word is a derived noun, not the verb; look for its prefix and pattern before glossing.
teach_template: A participle or other derived noun carries a shape (often a mīm prefix and a fixed pattern); show that shape and gloss it as the doer/done-to or a quality, never as the verb.
bottom_out_template: Name the derivative type and give a noun/adjective gloss, showing the prefix or pattern.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner glosses a derived noun with the same English verb it comes from, instead of describing the person or thing that does or receives the action.
A learner assumes every derived noun takes one fixed vowel pattern without first checking which class of verb it was built from.

arabic_grammar_name: dictionary infinitive leakage (tasarrub al-maṣdar al-muʿjamī)
plain_rule: A finite verb or a derived noun must not be glossed with the dictionary infinitive ('to ...'); the entry headword is a lookup form, not the token's contribution.
trigger_condition: a hover glosses an inflected token with the entry infinitive
expected_feature: a gloss that matches the token's actual form, not the entry 'to ...'
typical_error_feature: the dictionary 'to ...' pasted onto a finite or derived form
point_template: This is the entry's lookup form, not what the word says here; match the gloss to the actual form.
teach_template: The dictionary infinitive ('to write') is the lookup headword; the token in context is finite or derived, so gloss what it actually contributes, not the headword.
bottom_out_template: Give the gloss for the token's real form, and set the entry infinitive aside as lookup-only.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner copies the dictionary's 'to ...' gloss onto a verb that is actually conjugated in the text, instead of glossing the form that is actually there.

arabic_grammar_name: root radical vs. template augment (al-jadhr muqābil al-ḥarf al-zāʾid fī al-wazn)
plain_rule: A letter's role in a word -- root radical, or a letter the template itself adds -- is decided by the slot it fills once the word is matched to its template; it cannot be decided from the letter's shape alone, and counting the first three consonants of a word is not a reliable way to find its root.
trigger_condition: a word's root is named from its consonants, by shape or by counting, before the word is matched to a template
expected_feature: the word matched to its template first; a weak or extra-looking letter classified by the slot it occupies
typical_error_feature: a weak letter or a template-added letter treated as a root radical (or the reverse) by shape or position alone
point_template: Before you name this word's root, check which template it matches.
teach_template: A letter's role -- root radical or template-contributed addition -- is decided by the slot it fills once the word is matched to its template, not by the letter's shape and not by counting the first three consonants. Match the template first, then classify the letter.
bottom_out_template: Match the word to its template, then classify each letter by the slot -- radical or augment -- it occupies there.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner sees a weak letter in the middle of a word and calls it a root radical without first checking whether the matched template places an added letter in that exact position.
A learner counts a word's first three consonants and reports them as its root, without checking whether the matched template itself contributed one of those letters.

arabic_grammar_name: non-uniform verbal-noun template (maṣdar ghayr muṭṭarid li-l-fiʿl al-thulāthī)
plain_rule: A Form-I verb's verbal noun (maṣdar) has no single predictable shape; its exact template is a per-verb fact that must be checked, not derived from one assumed pattern.
trigger_condition: a Form-I verb's verbal-noun shape is assumed from one fixed template instead of checked per verb
expected_feature: the verbal noun's shape checked against the actual verb, not predicted from a single template
typical_error_feature: one uniform verbal-noun template applied to every Form-I verb
point_template: Before you gloss this verb's verbal noun, check its actual shape rather than assuming one pattern.
teach_template: The Form-I verbal noun (maṣdar) does not follow one uniform template across verbs -- two ordinary Form-I verbs can take two different shapes. Its exact form is a per-verb lexical fact and must be checked, not derived from a rule.
bottom_out_template: State the verb's actual attested verbal-noun shape rather than a predicted uniform template.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner assumes every Form-I verb's verbal noun follows the same shape and states a masdar the verb does not actually have.
A learner copies the verbal-noun pattern of one familiar verb onto a different verb of the same form, without checking whether that verb's actual masdar takes a different shape.

arabic_grammar_name: phrase gloss on a single token (tarjamat al-ʿibāra makāna al-kalima)
plain_rule: One token's hover must show that token's own contribution; a whole-phrase English translation borrowed from neighbouring words over-claims what the single token means.
trigger_condition: a token's hover carries a multi-word phrase translation that belongs to the surrounding words
expected_feature: the token's own contribution separated from the phrase context
typical_error_feature: a phrase gloss pinned to one token
point_template: This hover gives the whole phrase; ask what this single word contributes on its own.
teach_template: A neighbouring word may supply the subject, object, or relation; record that separately. The token's own hover shows only its piece, not the whole English phrase.
bottom_out_template: Give the token's own contribution, and name which neighbouring word supplies the rest of the phrase.

arabic_grammar_name: token outside the source-address graph (kharija ʿan al-ʿunwana al-maṣdariyya)
plain_rule: A hover claim needs a resolvable source address in the graph; a token that is not a graph node stays out of scope and cannot be certified from the surface alone.
trigger_condition: a claim targets a token with no source-address edge in the graph
expected_feature: the missing edge named and the claim held out of scope
typical_error_feature: a hover certified for a token that has no addressable home
point_template: Check that this token has a real source address before trusting the hover; here the address does not resolve.
teach_template: The engine certifies a hover against a source-addressed occurrence; when the token is not a node in the graph, name the missing edge and keep it out of scope rather than certifying from the surface.
bottom_out_template: Name the exact missing source-address edge and route the token to the validator lane.

arabic_grammar_name: display-local index mistaken for the canonical address (fahras maḥallī laysa al-ʿunwān al-qiyāsī)
plain_rule: A card-local word index that merely looks like sūrah:āyah:word is not the canonical address; a hover may be keyed only once the crosswalk to the canonical address exists.
trigger_condition: a hover is keyed to a display-local index with no crosswalk to the canonical address
expected_feature: the canonical crosswalk present before the hover is keyed
typical_error_feature: an orphan hover appended at a card-local index treated as canonical
point_template: Check whether this location is the canonical address or only a card-local index before keying the hover.
teach_template: Some cards number words with a card-local index that only looks canonical; before a hover is keyed, confirm the crosswalk to the real sūrah:āyah:word, or keep the row pending with the missing anchor.
bottom_out_template: Produce the crosswalk to the canonical address, or hold the row pending with the exact missing anchor.

arabic_grammar_name: public-boundary source leak (kharq ḥudūd al-naẓāfa al-ʿāmma)
plain_rule: A learner-facing gloss must be authored, never copied external source, brand, or provenance text; a boundary violation never ships.
trigger_condition: a hover or hint text carries copied external source/brand/provenance wording
expected_feature: authored, source-clean public text
typical_error_feature: external source wording pasted into the public gloss
point_template: This text carries wording that belongs to an internal source; the public gloss must be authored, not copied.
teach_template: Public learner text is authored in-house; source names, brands, and provenance labels route review internally but never become the public gloss. Rewrite the piece in your own words.
bottom_out_template: Replace the copied wording with an authored, source-clean gloss; a boundary violation never ships.

arabic_grammar_name: naʿt agreement licensing
plain_rule: An attributive follower (naʿt) copies its head noun's case, definiteness, gender and number, except a non-human plural head takes feminine-singular agreement and an indefinite, non-annexed elative stays in its invariable base shape.
trigger_condition: an adjective follows a noun and the agreement lattice cannot confirm all required axes from the supplied evidence
expected_feature: case, definiteness, gender and number copied from the head (or the two named exceptions correctly applied)
typical_error_feature: one agreement axis left uncopied, or an exception applied where it does not hold
point_template: Before assigning agreement here, name which axis the follower must copy.
teach_template: A naʿt copies its head's case, definiteness, gender and number, with two named exceptions; a right ending named without checking every axis is unsafe.
bottom_out_template: Name every agreement axis, then justify each one from the head.

arabic_grammar_name: ʿaṭf case-following and the light/heavy لكن split
plain_rule: A coordinated conjunct copies the case of the element it is joined to, whatever that case is; لَٰكِنَّ with gemination abrogates. Light لكن (no gemination) coordinates ONLY when it follows a negation/prohibition AND is followed by a single word; before an independent clause, or with no prior negation, light لكن is a non-governing adversative/ibtidāʾ particle, and the following noun's case comes from its own role in its own clause, never from case-copy onto لكن's conjunct.
trigger_condition: a coordinator joins two terms and the governor lattice cannot confirm the conjunct's case matches the joined-to element from the supplied evidence
expected_feature: the conjunct's case named as inherited from the joined-to element
typical_error_feature: the conjunct assigned a case of its own, or light لكن treated as a case-copying coordinator before an independent clause or with no prior negation/prohibition, without checking its licensing conditions
point_template: Before assigning the conjunct's case, name the element it is joined to.
teach_template: A conjunct never carries a case of its own; it copies the joined-to element's case, whatever that case is.
bottom_out_template: Name the joined-to element, then copy its case onto the conjunct.

arabic_grammar_name: badal (apposition) typology
plain_rule: An appositive (badal) copies its antecedent's case; total apposition needs no resumptive clitic, while partitive and inclusion apposition require one.
trigger_condition: a nominal follows another nominal sharing reference and the typology lattice cannot confirm the badal type from the supplied evidence
expected_feature: the badal type named (total/partitive/inclusion) with its case and clitic requirement
typical_error_feature: the badal's case assigned independently of its antecedent, or the clitic requirement of the partitive/inclusion types ignored
point_template: Before assigning a case here, name the badal type and its clitic requirement.
teach_template: A badal always copies its antecedent's case; only the partitive and inclusion types also require a resumptive clitic.
bottom_out_template: Name the badal type, then copy the antecedent's case and check the clitic.

arabic_grammar_name: wāw function discrimination (coordination vs. maʿiyya)
plain_rule: A nominal after وَ is an accompaniment (maʿiyya) object only with a verbal governor to its left; otherwise the wāw defaults to coordination and the second nominal copies the first noun's case. Animacy is a cue toward coordination, never an absolute gate against accompaniment.
trigger_condition: a nominal follows وَ and the sense lattice cannot confirm coordination vs. maʿiyya from the supplied evidence
expected_feature: a verbal governor checked before any accompaniment (accusative) reading
typical_error_feature: accompaniment asserted with no verbal governor, or ruled out from animacy alone
point_template: Before assigning a case after وَ, check for a verbal governor to its left.
teach_template: Maʿiyya needs a verbal governor; with none, the wāw coordinates and the second noun copies the first noun's case.
bottom_out_template: Check for a verbal governor, then decide coordination vs. accompaniment.

arabic_grammar_name: confusable letterforms (ḥurūf mutashābiha)
plain_rule: Two letters may look alike either because they share one skeleton and differ only by dot count and dot side, or because they belong to different families but happen to have a similar overall silhouette; either way, a letter's identity is read from its exact distinguishing feature (dots, stroke shape, or articulation), never assumed from a family resemblance.
trigger_condition: a learner names a letter from partial shape recognition without checking its distinguishing dots, stroke shape, or articulation
expected_feature: the letter's dot signature, stroke shape, or articulation checked before it is named
typical_error_feature: one member of a confusable pair read as the other from shape alone
point_template: Look again before naming this letter: a confusable partner shares much of its shape.
teach_template: Some letters share a skeleton and are told apart only by dot count and side; others belong to different families but share a similar silhouette and are told apart by stroke shape or articulation. Check the exact distinguishing feature before naming the letter.
bottom_out_template: Name the letter's distinguishing feature (dots, stroke, or articulation), then name the letter.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner reads دـ and رـ as the same letter because both drop a short curved stroke below the line, without checking the stroke's angle and depth.
A learner reads the emphatic ص as a plain س, missing that the emphasis changes the surrounding vowel quality and the word itself.

arabic_grammar_name: letter connectivity class (ḥurūf muttaṣila wa-ghayr muttaṣila)
plain_rule: Every letter belongs to one of two fixed connectivity classes: it either attaches to the letter that follows it, or it never does; that membership is a fixed fact about the letter, and it produces the visual runs and gaps a word is written in, which must be read correctly before word boundaries or medial letterforms are decided.
trigger_condition: a run boundary, gap, or medial letterform is read without checking the connectivity class of the letters involved
expected_feature: the connecting/non-connecting class checked before a run boundary, gap, or medial shape is interpreted
typical_error_feature: a non-connecting letter treated as connecting, or a gap/medial shape misread without checking connectivity
point_template: Check this letter's connectivity class before deciding what the shapes around it mean.
teach_template: Every letter is fixed as connecting or non-connecting; a non-connector produces a gap and a medial letter can look identical to another family member until its dots are read. Decide connectivity and dots before reading a run boundary or a letter's identity.
bottom_out_template: State the letter's connectivity class, then read the run or gap it produces.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner draws a connecting stroke from a non-connecting letter into the letter that follows it, fusing two separate glyph shapes into one.
A learner reads a gap produced by a non-connecting letter as the end of a word, splitting one word into two.

arabic_grammar_name: short-vowel diacritics and vocalization state (al-ḥarakāt wa-ḥālat al-tashkīl)
plain_rule: The three short-vowel marks are told apart by their position on the letter, not their shape, and a written position carries a vowel only when a mark actually licenses one there; most ordinary Arabic text is unmarked, and the reader supplies the missing vowels from pattern and context rather than expecting or inventing marks that are not written.
trigger_condition: a vowel is read from a mark's shape rather than its position, or a vowel is expected or invented where none is written
expected_feature: vowel marks read by position, and unmarked positions left unfilled unless context licenses a specific reading
typical_error_feature: fatḥa and kasra swapped by shape, vowel marks expected on every word, or a vowel invented where none is marked
point_template: Check the position of this mark, and whether a mark is even written here, before reading a vowel.
teach_template: Fatḥa sits above the letter and kasra sits below it, though both are drawn as the same short stroke; ḍamma marks a short u and needs an added carrier letter for length; most Arabic text carries no marks at all, so the reader supplies vowels from pattern and context rather than inventing one where nothing is written.
bottom_out_template: State the mark's position (or its absence) and the vowel or vocalization state it licenses.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner swaps the a-mark and the i-mark because both are drawn as the same short diagonal stroke, without checking whether the stroke sits above or below the letter.
A learner inserts a vowel between two consonants that carry no vowel mark at all, changing the word's syllable count.

arabic_grammar_name: sukūn and shadda marks (al-sukūn wa-l-shadda)
plain_rule: Sukūn and shadda are opposite instructions written as small superscript marks over a consonant: sukūn forbids a following vowel and closes the syllable, while shadda doubles the consonant and is read together with whatever vowel mark is stacked on it; neither mark may be read as a neutral placeholder or reduced to only half of what it says.
trigger_condition: a sukūn or shadda mark is read as optional, confused with the other mark, or read without its stacked vowel
expected_feature: sukūn read as forbidding a vowel and shadda read as doubling the consonant together with its stacked vowel
typical_error_feature: a vowel inserted after sukūn, sukūn and shadda confused, gemination realized without its vowel, or gemination collapsed to a single consonant
point_template: Look at this small mark again: sukūn and shadda say opposite things about the consonant.
teach_template: Sukūn (a closed circle) forbids a following vowel; shadda (a head-shaped stroke) doubles the consonant and is always read together with whatever vowel is stacked on it. Neither mark is decorative, and dropping half of what shadda says, the doubling or its vowel, changes the word.
bottom_out_template: Name the mark, state what it licenses or forbids, and read any vowel stacked with it.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner pronounces a single short vowel after a sukūn-marked consonant, contradicting the mark's own instruction that no vowel follows.
A learner reads a shadda-marked consonant as a single short consonant, dropping the doubling the mark licenses.

arabic_grammar_name: long-vowel carrier letters (ḥurūf al-madd)
plain_rule: Wāw and yāʾ are each ambiguous between a full consonant role and a long-vowel carrier role, and the role is decided by the mark configuration around the letter, not by habit; vowel length itself is contrastive, so a long vowel must never be shortened, and a word-final dotless yāʾ-shaped grapheme is a positional spelling variant of long ā, not a yāʾ.
trigger_condition: wāw, yāʾ, or a word-final dotless yāʾ-shaped grapheme is read without checking its mark configuration, or a long vowel is shortened in speech
expected_feature: the carrier/consonant role decided from the mark configuration, and vowel length preserved
typical_error_feature: wāw or yāʾ assumed to be always a vowel or always a consonant, a word-final dotless yāʾ-shape misread as long ī, or a long vowel shortened in speech
point_template: Check the marks around this wāw or yāʾ before deciding whether it is a consonant or a long-vowel carrier.
teach_template: Wāw and yāʾ are consonants when they carry their own vowel mark, and long-vowel carriers when unmarked right after the matching short vowel; a dotless word-final yāʾ-shape is a spelling of long ā, not a yāʾ; and vowel length is contrastive, so it is never shortened for convenience.
bottom_out_template: State the mark configuration, name the role it licenses, and preserve the vowel's length.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner reads a dotless word-final yāʾ-shaped grapheme as a long ī because it shares yāʾ's skeleton, missing that it is a positional spelling of long ā.
A learner shortens a long vowel in speech, treating vowel length as a matter of speaking style rather than a contrastive part of the word.

arabic_grammar_name: written realization of nunation (rasm al-tanwīn)
plain_rule: Nunation is a doubled short-vowel mark written at a word's final edge that adds a nasal ending, and it is never realized the same way as gemination, which doubles a stem consonant instead; the a-form of nunation additionally needs a silent supporting alif on an ordinary consonant-final word, decided from the word's own final grapheme against a short exempt list, not from how the ending sounds.
trigger_condition: nunation is conflated with gemination, its supporting alif is read as audible or dropped where required, or the support requirement is decided by ear instead of by the word's final grapheme
expected_feature: nunation located at the word edge and distinguished from stem-internal gemination, and the supporting alif's requirement and silence both honored
typical_error_feature: nunation and gemination conflated, the supporting alif pronounced as a vowel, or the supporting alif omitted where the final grapheme requires it
point_template: Look again at this word-final ending: nunation, gemination, and the supporting alif each say something different.
teach_template: Nunation is a doubled vowel mark at the word's edge that adds a nasal ending, never the same thing as gemination on a stem consonant. Its a-form needs a silent supporting alif on an ordinary consonant-final word (decided from the word's own final grapheme, not by ear), and that alif itself is never pronounced.
bottom_out_template: Locate the mark, name whether it is nunation or gemination, and state the supporting-alif requirement from the word's final grapheme.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner pronounces the silent supporting alif written under the a-form of nunation as an extra vowel sound.
A learner conflates the word-final doubled-vowel mark of nunation with the gemination mark written over a stem consonant.

arabic_grammar_name: assimilation of the definite article's lām (idghām lām al-taʿrīf)
plain_rule: The definite article's lām assimilates only before the closed set of sun letters, merging into the following consonant as gemination rather than being deleted, and it stays audible before every moon letter; class membership is fixed and memorized, never derived from spelling or extended by analogy.
trigger_condition: the article's lām is pronounced or silenced, or gemination is applied or withheld, without first checking the following letter's sun/moon class membership
expected_feature: the following letter's sun/moon membership checked first, with gemination applied only for sun letters and the lām kept audible only for moon letters
typical_error_feature: gemination extended to a moon letter by analogy, the lām dropped without geminating the following consonant, sun/moon membership confused, or the lām pronounced before a sun letter
point_template: Before you decide whether the lām is heard here, name the following letter's class.
teach_template: The article's lām assimilates only before the closed set of sun letters, merging into that consonant as gemination, not vanishing; before every moon letter it stays audible instead. The two classes are fixed lists that must be memorized, never derived from the spelling or extended by analogy.
bottom_out_template: Name the following letter's class, then state whether the lām is audible or merged as gemination.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner adds gemination after the article's lām before a moon letter, extending the sun-letter pattern by analogy.
A learner drops the article's lām before a sun letter without doubling the following consonant, treating assimilation as deletion rather than merger.

arabic_grammar_name: assimilated (mithāl) verb — Form I imperfect first-radical deletion
plain_rule: In Form I only, an assimilated verb whose first radical is wāw deletes that radical in the imperfect when the stem vowel is /i/ or /u/; the derived-form/imperative rebuilding this deletion licenses is scoped to that same Form I imperfect cell — it is never extended to Forms II-X, to the corresponding imperative of a stem that already opens on a voweled consonant, or read back as if a derived form's retained first radical meant the verb was still Form I.
trigger_condition: a Form I assimilated verb's imperfect, imperative, or a derived-form (II-X) cell built on the same root is being formed and the deletion rule's Form-I-only scope has not been checked
expected_feature: the imperfect first-radical deletion applied only to the Form I imperfect cell it is licensed for, with derived forms and the imperative correctly excluded or re-derived from their own template
typical_error_feature: the deletion extended to a derived (II-X) form, a prosthetic hamza added to an imperative stem that already opens on a voweled consonant, or a derived form's retained first radical misread as evidence the verb is still Form I
point_template: Before you touch the first radical, check which form (I or derived) and which cell (imperfect/imperative) you are actually building.
teach_template: First-radical wāw-deletion is a Form I imperfect fact only; the imperative built from a deleted stem needs no prosthetic hamza, derived forms (II-X) keep the first radical because they never delete it, and a retained first radical after a derived-form prefix is not a sign the verb reverted to Form I.
bottom_out_template: Name the form and the cell, then state whether first-radical deletion applies there.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner treats the Form I imperfect deletion rule as if it applied to a Form II-X verb sharing the same root, wrongly dropping the first radical from a derived form that never deletes it.

arabic_grammar_name: defective (nāqiṣ) verb — subtype vowel, jussive deletion, and suffix-triggered shift
plain_rule: A defective verb's imperfect middle/final vowel is a lexically stored subtype fact, never interchangeable between subtypes; its jussive/imperative is formed by deleting the final weak radical outright rather than adding sukūn to it; and a consonant-initial suffix on the past stem (e.g. the masculine plural wāw) forces the weak final radical to shift/reappear rather than leaving the bare past's long vowel in place.
trigger_condition: a defective verb's imperfect subtype vowel, its jussive/imperative form, or a suffixed past cell is being produced and the subtype-specific vowel, the deletion rule, or the suffix-triggered shift has not been checked against this verb's own lexical entry
expected_feature: the subtype's own stored vowel used (never swapped for the other subtype's), the final weak radical deleted (not merely marked with sukūn) under a jussive/imperative operator, and the suffix-triggered shift applied before a consonant-initial suffix
typical_error_feature: the two subtype vowels exchanged, the final weak consonant kept visible under a jussive operator, or a suffixed past cell written with the bare past's long alif instead of the shifted consonant the suffix licenses
point_template: Before you write this cell, check the verb's own subtype vowel and whether a jussive operator or a consonant-initial suffix is acting on it.
teach_template: Nāqiṣ subtype vowels are stored per verb, not interchangeable; the jussive/imperative is exponed by deleting the final radical outright; and a consonant-initial suffix forces the underlying weak radical back, so the bare past's long vowel is not available in that cell.
bottom_out_template: Name the subtype vowel, then state what the jussive/imperative or the suffix does to the final radical.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner writes the masculine plural past of a defective verb with the bare past's final long vowel instead of the consonant the suffix forces back, producing a non-existent past-tense cell.

arabic_grammar_name: geminate (muḍaʿʿaf) verb — merger/separation licensing and the jussive shapes
plain_rule: A geminate verb's imperfect vowel is a lexically stored fact, not predictable from the class; its gemination realizes two root consonants and is never dropped as if optional; the two identical radicals merge only where the following element is NOT a bare consonant-initial suffix, and separate only where a consonant-initial suffix follows — reversing this licensing stacks or drops a radical; and merged-with-fatḥa and separated-with-sukūn are two SECURELY licensed jussive shapes of a geminate verb (a merged form with ḍamma is simply the indicative, not a jussive option at all) — this pair is taught as securely licensed examples, not as a claim that they exhaust the complete classical geminate-jussive inventory; a further merged-vowel variant is an open scholar-review question this KC does not settle.
trigger_condition: a geminate verb's imperfect vowel, its merger/separation, or its jussive shape is being produced and the per-verb vowel or the suffix-conditioned merger licensing has not been checked
expected_feature: the verb's own stored imperfect vowel used, merger applied only where no consonant-initial suffix follows and separation only where one does, and the jussive limited to its securely licensed shapes
typical_error_feature: one uniform imperfect vowel assumed for the whole class, the gemination mark dropped as if decorative, merger and separation licensing reversed against the following suffix, or an indicative-shaped (ḍamma) merged form mistaken for a jussive
point_template: Before you write this cell, check the verb's own stored vowel and what actually follows the second radical.
teach_template: The geminate imperfect vowel is stored per verb; gemination realizes two radicals and is never optional; a consonant-initial suffix forces separation and blocks merger; and merged-with-fatḥa and separated-with-sukūn are two securely licensed jussive shapes — a merged-with-ḍamma form is the indicative, not a jussive option — without this being a claim that no other merged-vowel shape is ever licensed.
bottom_out_template: State the stored vowel, then justify merger or separation from what follows, then name the licensed jussive shape.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner keeps a geminate verb's two identical radicals merged even though a consonant-initial suffix follows, stacking a doubled consonant against a vowelless one.

arabic_grammar_name: hamzated (mahmūz) verb — carrier selection and stored irregular cells
plain_rule: A hamzated verb's hamza carrier is selected by the vowels in its immediate environment, never a free spelling choice, and that carrier is re-evaluated after every affixation; a small closed set of hamzated verbs additionally have stored irregular imperatives (formed without the hamza) and, for one member, a stored irregular imperfect with no hamza at all — lexical facts to check, not outputs of the regular carrier rule; and a hamza radical is a separate class from the weak (wāw/yāʾ) radicals, so weak-root rules never transfer to it.
trigger_condition: a hamzated verb's carrier, its imperative, its imperfect, or its root classification is being decided and the vowel-environment carrier rule, the small stored-irregular list, or the hamza-vs-weak-root distinction has not been checked
expected_feature: the carrier chosen from the immediate vowel environment and re-checked after affixation, the stored irregular imperatives (and the one stored irregular imperfect) used as lexical facts rather than derived, and a hamza radical never treated as a weak radical
typical_error_feature: the wrong carrier chosen or kept unchanged after a plural suffix, a regular hamza restored into a cell that is lexically hamza-less, or a hamza-bearing root run through a weak-root rule
point_template: Before you write the hamza, check the vowels immediately around it and whether this cell is one of the small stored-irregular ones.
teach_template: The hamza carrier is decided by its immediate vowel environment and must be re-checked after every affixation; a short stored list of hamzated verbs has irregular imperatives (and one an irregular imperfect) with no hamza at all; and a hamza radical is a separate class from the weak radicals, so weak-root rules do not transfer to it.
bottom_out_template: Name the carrier from its vowel environment (or the stored irregular form), then confirm the root's class is hamza, not weak.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner restores a regular hamza into the imperfect of one of the few hamzated verbs that are lexically stored without a hamza there at all.

arabic_grammar_name: doubly weak (lafīf) verb — subtype composition
plain_rule: A lafīf verb's subtype (maqrūn/mafrūq — which two positions carry the weak radicals) is assigned from the positions of its weak radicals before conjugating, and the two subtypes' imperfect stems differ in shape AND length; the separated (mafrūq) subtype deletes its first weak radical in the imperfect exactly as a plain first-weak (assimilated) verb does, so restoring it produces a non-word; a lafīf verb's jussive still deletes its final weak radical, exactly as an ordinary defective verb's does; and in the indefinite, its active participle's final radical gives way to tanwīn — writing that radical as a visible consonant there is a spelling error, not a variant.
trigger_condition: a lafīf verb's subtype, its imperfect stem, its jussive, or its indefinite active-participle spelling is being produced and the subtype has not been fixed from the weak-radical positions first
expected_feature: the subtype assigned from radical position before conjugating, the correct (subtype-specific) imperfect stem produced, the final weak radical deleted under the jussive, and the indefinite participle spelled with tanwīn in place of the final radical
typical_error_feature: the two subtypes' imperfect shapes conflated, the mafrūq subtype's first weak radical wrongly restored into the imperfect, the final weak radical kept visible under a jussive operator, or the indefinite active participle written with a visible final radical instead of tanwīn
point_template: Before you conjugate a lafīf verb, fix its subtype from the positions of its two weak radicals.
teach_template: Lafīf subtype is decided by radical position first; maqrūn and mafrūq imperfects differ in shape and length; the mafrūq subtype deletes its first radical in the imperfect exactly like a plain assimilated verb; the jussive still deletes the final radical exactly like a plain defective verb; and the indefinite active participle spells tanwīn where the final radical would be, never the radical itself.
bottom_out_template: Name the subtype, then justify the imperfect stem, the jussive, or the indefinite spelling from it.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner conjugates a lafīf verb's imperfect without first checking whether its two weak radicals are in the maqrūn or mafrūq positions, producing the wrong stem shape and length.

arabic_grammar_name: passive voice melody (bināʾ lil-majhūl) and promoted-argument case/agreement, in weak-root stems
plain_rule: Voice is carried entirely by the vowel melody (the prefix vowel together with the vowel before the final radical, or — for a medial-weak stem — its own distinct passive melody), never by argument marking alone; a medial-weak (hollow) stem takes its own passive melody and rejects the sound-stem melody; once an argument is promoted to fill the missing agent slot, it takes the case a subject takes (nominative, never left accusative) and controls agreement exactly as an agent would, including the feminine-singular pattern for a non-human plural; and an active melody left in place states an active proposition however the arguments are marked.
trigger_condition: a passive clause's verb melody, or the case/agreement of its promoted argument, is being produced for a weak-root (specifically medial-weak/hollow) stem and the melody or the promotion consequence has not been checked
expected_feature: the correct passive melody used for the stem's own class (including the hollow stem's own passive melody), the promoted argument marked nominative, and agreement controlled by the promoted argument
typical_error_feature: the ordinary (sound-stem) passive melody applied to a medial-weak stem, the active prefix vowel kept in the imperfect passive, an active melody paired with passive-looking argument marking, the promoted argument left accusative, or the passive verb left unagreed with its promoted argument
point_template: Before you assign case or agreement here, check the verb's own melody first — voice is decided there.
teach_template: Voice is exponed by the vowel melody, not by argument marking; a hollow (medial-weak) stem has its own passive melody, never the sound-stem one; once promoted, the argument takes the subject's case (nominative) and controls agreement exactly as an agent would; and an active melody always states an active proposition, regardless of how the arguments happen to be marked.
bottom_out_template: Name the melody first, then justify the promoted argument's case and agreement from it.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner applies the ordinary sound-stem passive melody to a medial-weak (hollow) verb instead of that stem's own distinct passive melody.

arabic_grammar_name: deputy agent (nāʾib al-fāʿil) function discrimination
plain_rule: The deputy agent is identified by case and position — the nominative element occupying the subject position of a passive verb — never by translating into a language whose passive uses a by-phrase; a following prepositional phrase is a separate constituent in the genitive and is never itself the deputy agent; the deputy agent controls agreement exactly as an agent does, including the feminine-singular pattern for a non-human plural; once promoted, an element takes the case a subject takes (nominative), never the accusative case it had in the active sentence; and the verb's melody must itself be set to passive.
trigger_condition: a passive clause's subject-position element, or the agreement/case it carries, is being identified and a following prepositional phrase, an unagreed verb, a leftover accusative case, or the verb's own melody has not been checked
expected_feature: the deputy agent identified by case and position (not by a by-phrase translation), a following PP correctly excluded as a separate genitive constituent, agreement and nominative case correctly assigned to the deputy agent, and the verb's melody confirmed passive
typical_error_feature: a following prepositional phrase mistaken for the deputy agent, the passive verb left unagreed with its actual deputy agent, the promoted element left in the accusative case it had in the active sentence, or an active verb melody used with a nominative patient
point_template: Before you name the deputy agent, check case and position first, then confirm the verb's own melody is passive.
teach_template: The deputy agent is the nominative element in the passive subject position, found from case and position, never from a by-phrase translation; a following PP is a separate genitive constituent, not the deputy agent; it controls agreement like any agent; it takes nominative case, never the accusative it had actively; and the verb's melody itself must be passive for any of this to cohere.
bottom_out_template: Name the deputy agent by case and position, confirm the verb's melody is passive, then justify its case and agreement.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner names the object of a following prepositional phrase as the deputy agent instead of the nominative element actually occupying the passive subject position.
